synopsis: Diagnostic coverage is the proportion of dangerous failures detected by the system itself; dead time includes undetected faults, start-up before self-tests finish, sensor blindness and degraded or switched-off operation [f12124, f12125, f12128]. Achieved Performance Level depends partly on diagnostic coverage, with ISO 13849 bands of none below 60%, low from 60–90%, medium from 90–99%, and high at 99% or above [f12025, f12126]. ISO 16001:2017 requires start-up self-checking and continuous fault monitoring, while off-road contamination makes sensor self-diagnosis and degradation detection particularly important [f2411, f2412, f2002]. MOSH requires disconnection detection within 500 ms, but the booklet's critical-fault wording differs between reaching safety within 500 ms after detection and detecting the failure and reaching safety within 500 ms; planners should resolve that timing distinction [f5284, f12102, f12132]. No published off-road acceptance value for availability or diagnostic coverage was found, so the booklet recommends measuring availability, time in degraded mode and fault-detection coverage rather than relying on detection rates measured only while available [f12133, f2633, f5441, f12129]. HIL data injection can test diagnostics and fail-to-safe behaviour, but treating degraded sensing as a fault can increase stops, and excessive stops or alarms risk operators switching systems off [f5697, f12134, f12135].
